title: What must workers be trained on for high risk construction work and SWMS in Australia?
seoTitle: SWMS and high risk construction work
description: Model WHS Regulations r 291 to 303 on high risk construction work and SWMS: the 18 activities, SWMS content, and what workers must understand before starting.
shortAnswer: Under Part 6.3 of Australia's model Work Health and Safety Regulations, a business carrying out any of 18 categories of high risk construction work must have a safe work method statement (SWMS) before the work starts, ensure the work follows it, and stop work that does not. The model Code of Practice: Construction work says workers should understand the hazards and risks, understand and implement the SWMS controls, and know what to do if work departs from the SWMS.
keyTakeaways: Regulation 291 defines high risk construction work as 18 categories, including a risk of falling more than 2 meters, trenches deeper than 1.5 meters, work near energized electrical services, tilt-up and precast concrete, and work where powered mobile plant moves.

Regulation 299 requires a SWMS before the work starts that identifies the work, specifies hazards and risks, describes controls and describes how they will be implemented, monitored and reviewed, expressed so that users can understand it.
Regulation 300 requires arrangements to ensure the work follows the SWMS, and requires work that departs from it to stop immediately or as soon as safe.

Workers and their health and safety representatives must be consulted when a SWMS is prepared and reviewed, and the Code treats the briefing on a SWMS as information and instruction delivered at induction, site training or toolbox talks.
A SWMS must be kept until the work is complete, or for at least 2 years after a notifiable incident, and be readily accessible to workers doing the work.
jurisdiction: Australia (model WHS laws, adopted in all jurisdictions except Victoria)
regulator: Safe Work Australia (model laws) and state and territory WHS regulators
appliesTo: PCBUs whose business or undertaking includes carrying out high risk construction work, including builders, subcontractors and self-employed tradespeople
Principal contractors for construction projects of $250,000 or more
Workers, leading hands and supervisors carrying out or overseeing high risk construction work
Health and safety representatives consulted on SWMS

sections.heading: What counts as high risk construction work?

blocks.text: Construction work that falls into any of the 18 categories in regulation 291 of the [model Work Health and Safety Regulations](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/doc/model-work-health-and-safety-regulations). Safe Work Australia's [construction risk guidance](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/safety-topic/industry-and-business/construction/managing-risks) restates the same list. In summary, high risk construction work is construction work that:

items: involves a risk of a person falling more than 2 meters
is carried out on a telecommunication tower
involves demolition of a load-bearing element or one related to the structure's physical integrity
involves, or is likely to involve, the disturbance of asbestos
involves structural alterations or repairs that need temporary support to prevent collapse
is carried out in or near a confined space
is carried out in or near a shaft or trench deeper than 1.5 meters, or a tunnel
involves the use of explosives
is carried out on or near pressurized gas distribution mains or piping, or chemical, fuel or refrigerant lines
is carried out on or near energized electrical installations or services
is carried out where there may be a contaminated or flammable atmosphere
involves tilt-up or precast concrete
is carried out on, in or next to a road, railway, shipping lane or other traffic corridor in use by traffic other than pedestrians
is carried out where powered mobile plant moves
is carried out in areas with artificial extremes of temperature
is carried out in or near water or other liquid with a risk of drowning
involves diving work

blocks.text: The list above groups gas mains and chemical, fuel or refrigerant lines in one line; regulation 291 lists them separately, giving 18 categories. Safe Work Australia's [SWMS information sheet](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/doc/safe-work-method-statement-high-risk-construction-work-information-sheet) says a SWMS is not required for work of a minor nature, and that one SWMS can cover several high risk activities in the same task.

blocks.title: Currency
blocks.text: This page reflects the model WHS Regulations (December 5, 2025 version), the model Code of Practice: Construction work (November 2024) and Safe Work Australia's SWMS information sheet, as at November 2026. The model laws apply in every jurisdiction except Victoria, and each jurisdiction's regulation may differ in numbering and penalties.

Four things, set out in regulation 299(2): it must identify the work that is high risk construction work; specify the hazards and the associated risks to health and safety; describe the measures to control the risks; and describe how the control measures are to be implemented, monitored and reviewed.

Regulation 299(3) adds two conditions that matter for training. The SWMS must be prepared taking into account the circumstances at the workplace and, on a construction project, the principal contractor's WHS management plan. And it must "be set out and expressed in a way that is readily accessible and understandable to persons who use it." Safe Work Australia's information sheet says a SWMS "must be easily understood by workers, including those from non-English speaking backgrounds", suggests pictures or diagrams, and warns that a lengthy, overly detailed SWMS can be hard to understand and apply.

The information sheet also describes a SWMS as an administrative control that supports higher order controls, not a procedure. It is a tool "to help supervisors and workers confirm and monitor the control measures required at the workplace." A generic SWMS can be used for recurring work only if reviewed and revised for the specific workplace.

sections.heading: What must workers be trained on before high risk construction work?

blocks.text: They must understand the SWMS for their task well enough to follow it and to stop when it is not being followed. Section 4.3 of the [model Code of Practice: Construction work](https://www.safeworkaustralia.gov.au/doc/model-code-practice-construction-work) says workers engaged in high risk construction work should:

items: understand the hazards and risks arising from the work
understand and implement the risk controls in a SWMS
know what to do if the work is not being conducted in accordance with the SWMS

blocks.text: The Code says this information and instruction "may be provided during general construction induction training, workplace-specific training or during a toolbox talk by the principal contractor, contractor or subcontractor." The third point connects directly to regulation 300(2), which requires work that departs from the SWMS to be "stopped immediately or as soon as it is safe to do so" and resumed only in accordance with the statement. A worker who has not been told this cannot be expected to act on it.

Supervisors carry a larger share. The Code says workers in a supervisory role, such as a leading hand or foreman, "should be trained and authorised to ensure the work is carried out in accordance with relevant policies, procedures and the SWMS," and that responsibility to implement, monitor and review controls may be allocated to a supervisor, although the business's duty is not transferable. The general duty to provide information, training and instruction comes from regulation 39, covered on the [WHS Act training duty](/regulations/whs-act-duty-to-provide-training) page.

sections.heading: How must workers be involved when a SWMS is prepared or changed?

blocks.text: Workers and their health and safety representatives must be consulted when a SWMS is prepared and when it is reviewed. The Code says that if no workers are engaged at the planning stage, consultation must happen when the SWMS is first made available to workers, "for example during workplace-specific training or a toolbox talk", and that a SWMS may record who was consulted, when, and their signature.

Regulation 302 requires a SWMS to be reviewed and as necessary revised whenever the relevant control measures are revised under regulation 38. The Code then expects workers to be told a revision was made and how to access it, people who must change a procedure to be told in a way that lets them implement it, and workers to get the information and instruction needed to apply the revised SWMS. On a construction project the principal contractor must be given a copy of the revised SWMS. Each revision is therefore a retraining event, not just a document update. See [how to update training when regulations change](/guides/how-to-update-training-when-regulations-change) for a method that also works for procedure changes.

sections.heading: What extra duties does a principal contractor have?

blocks.text: On a construction project, which regulation 292 defines as one where the construction work costs $250,000 or more, the principal contractor must take all reasonable steps to obtain each SWMS before the high risk work starts (regulation 312), and each subcontractor must give it a copy before starting (regulation 301).

The principal contractor's written WHS management plan must include "the arrangements for the collection and any assessment, monitoring and review of safe work method statements" (regulation 309(2)(e)). Regulation 310 requires the principal contractor, so far as reasonably practicable, to make each person who will carry out construction work on the project aware of the plan's content and their right to inspect it before they start, which is usually done at site induction.

sections.heading: How long must a SWMS be kept, and who must be able to see it?

blocks.text: Until the high risk construction work is complete, or at least 2 years after a notifiable incident connected with it. Regulation 303 also requires the SWMS to be readily accessible to any worker engaged to carry out the work for that period, and available for inspection under the Act. The Code says every version should be kept when a SWMS is revised, and Safe Work Australia's information sheet notes it can be kept electronically. Evidence that workers were briefed is separate from the SWMS itself; for record design see [how to prepare training records for an audit](/guides/how-to-prepare-training-records-for-an-audit).

sections.heading: How can a builder map SWMS duties to training and evidence?

blocks.text: Map each duty to the role that carries it, the moment it is triggered, and evidence that a worker understood the SWMS, not only signed it. The table below is an original, illustrative mapping.

blocks.text: The white card that every worker must hold before construction work is covered separately on the [general construction induction](/regulations/general-construction-induction-white-card) page. Specific HRCW categories have their own training rules, for example [confined space training](/regulations/confined-space-training-requirements) and [asbestos training](/regulations/asbestos-removal-and-awareness-training-australia).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry treats each SWMS as a structured set of hazards, controls and responsibilities linked to the roles that apply them. Briefings and checks are built from that structure, so when a control is revised, the workers who need re-briefing and the assessment points that change are identified automatically.

faqs.q: Is signing a SWMS the same as being trained on it?
faqs.a: No. The model Regulations require the SWMS to be understandable to its users and the work to follow it. The Code expects workers to understand the hazards, implement the controls and know what to do if work departs from the SWMS. A signature can record consultation or a briefing, but it does not show understanding on its own.

faqs.q: Does every construction task need a SWMS?
faqs.a: No. A SWMS is required only for the 18 categories of high risk construction work in regulation 291. Safe Work Australia says it is not required for work of a minor nature, though other construction work still requires risks to be managed so far as is reasonably practicable.

faqs.q: Who should write the SWMS on a subcontracted job?
faqs.a: Safe Work Australia's information sheet says the person responsible for carrying out the high risk work is best placed to prepare it, in consultation with the workers who will do the work. Generally that means the builder for its own workers, or the subcontractor for its workers. The principal contractor, builder and subcontractors should agree who is best placed.

faqs.q: Can a generic SWMS be used across sites?
faqs.a: Only after it is reviewed for the specific workplace. The Code and Safe Work Australia's information sheet both say a generic SWMS may not meet the law unless reviewed for the hazards and risks of the particular site and revised as necessary, and workers must then be briefed on the site specific version.
